title: networking-streaming-http-grpc-proxies-chunking-benchmarks-2025
content:
Purpose:
Run controlled experiments to quantify networking and streaming overheads in the serving runtime. Focus areas: HTTP vs gRPC streaming, chunking strategies, backpressure behavior, and proxy (Envoy) impact under representative LLM workloads.

High-level summary (TL;DR):
- gRPC streaming has slightly better median latency than HTTP/1.1 chunked streaming for small-chunk workloads (~0.5–1.2ms lower median), but differences narrow with larger chunk sizes and batching.
- Envoy proxy introduces a consistent median add of ~0.7–1.5ms and increases p99 by ~5–12ms depending on buffer/window settings.
- Very small chunk sizes (<=512B token chunks) drive CPU + syscalls up and increase p95/p99 dramatically — avoid sub-1KB chunking for high QPS.
- Backpressure (client-windowing + server batching) reduces tail for gRPC streaming by ~20–30% at high QPS vs naive unthrottled streaming.

Experimental setup:
- Hardware: 4x c6i.4xlarge clients (Linux), Server: 1x g5.2xlarge with model runner pinned to a single GPU. Network: 10Gbps NIC, no external WAN.
- Software: serving-runtime main@v0.31.2, model: small encoder-decoder reference (seq len 512), TLS enabled (AES-GCM), Envoy 1.28 used where noted.
- Workloads: three workload profiles
  * interactive_small: 1–4 tokens per chunk, 40 reqs/sec per client, low latency SLO
  * interactive_medium: 8–64 tokens per chunk, 200 reqs/sec per client
  * batching_throughput: large responses (200–600 tokens), high concurrency to saturate GPU throughput
- Metrics captured: per-request latency (start->first-token, per-chunk arrival), p50/p95/p99, throughput (tokens/s), CPU (user/sys), network bytes tx/rx, system call counts (write/send), connection reuse stats.

Methodology notes:
- Each experiment run = 30 minutes with 10 minute warmup. Reported numbers are from steady-state period.
- For HTTP we tested two modes: HTTP/1.1 chunked streaming (server push of chunked bodies) and HTTP/2 with streaming data frames.
- For gRPC we used bidi streaming and server-stream responses with chunked proto messages.
- Envoy runs were simple TCP proxying with default HTTP filters; we also tested with tuned proxy buffers and with drain/discard policies to simulate misconfiguration.

Key results (representative numbers, median/p95/p99 in ms):
1) interactive_small (clients x4):
  - gRPC (no proxy): median=6.5ms, p95=18.2ms, p99=38.1ms
  - HTTP/1.1 chunked: median=7.7ms, p95=23.9ms, p99=48.4ms
  - HTTP/2: median=7.1ms, p95=20.4ms, p99=42.9ms
  - gRPC + Envoy: median=8.3ms, p95=29.6ms, p99=60.0ms
  - Notes: system call rate (send) for HTTP/1.1 chunked ~1.3x gRPC due to framing overhead for tiny writes.

2) interactive_medium:
  - gRPC (no proxy): median=9.8ms, p95=28.0ms, p99=55.2ms
  - HTTP/1.1 chunked: median=10.4ms, p95=30.6ms, p99=62.0ms
  - gRPC + Envoy: median=11.6ms, p95=36.1ms, p99=78.8ms
  - Notes: chunking at 16–64 token sizes shows best tradeoff for median+tail.

3) batching_throughput (saturate GPU):
  - gRPC streaming (large chunks): throughput ~420k tokens/s, median request-latency=120ms (GPU dominated)
  - HTTP proxying path reduces tokens/s by ~3–6% depending on buffer sizing due to extra copy and epoll wakeups

Chunk size sensitivity (same workload):
- 256B chunks: p95/p99 blow up (p95 +35%, p99 +65%) vs 4KB chunks — overhead dominated by more syscalls, framing, and TLS record boundaries.
- 1KB–8KB chunks: sweet spot for balancing latency and CPU. 4KB slightly better for throughput-heavy workloads.

Backpressure and windowing experiments:
- Naive client (streams as produced): under high concurrency server queues lead to unbounded buffering at proxy; p99 increases >2x.
- Client-side windowing (limit outstanding chunks) + server batching: reduces p99 by 20–30% at high QPS and avoids proxy memory pressure.
- gRPC flow-control is effective when clients respect window updates; HTTP/2 does similar but many client libs default to large windows which can delay backpressure signals.

Proxy-specific behavior (Envoy):
- Default Envoy config introduces modest median overhead but amplifies tail when upstream is slow (due to internal buffering + thread wakeups).
- Tuned buffer limits (reduce max pending bytes per-connection) and enabling write coalescing reduces p99 by ~8–15%.
- Misconfigured proxies (large per-connection buffers, slow drain) can double p99 under bursty traffic.

Observability findings (where we lost signal):
- Per-chunk metrics are crucial — aggregated request-level only hides per-chunk stalls that drive tail latency.
- TLS record boundaries correlate with unexpected latency spikes; recommend logging TLS record sizes for troubleshooting.

Quick recommendations (engineering actionables):
1) Default chunking: 1KB–4KB for hosted API streaming; expose as config and include recommended presets (interactive vs throughput).
2) gRPC as default streaming protocol for internal interpolation between services. HTTP/2 OK for external clients but document chunk-size pitfalls.
3) Proxy defaults: reduce per-connection buffer limits, enable coalescing; add a CI benchmark for Envoy config changes.
4) Implement client-side windowing sample in SDKs (JS/Python) with sane defaults to avoid runaway outstanding chunks.
5) Improve runtime observability: emit per-chunk arrival timestamps, TLS record size histogram, and proxy queue-length gauges.

Open questions / next experiments:
- Repeat whole-suite over WAN (multi-region) to quantify RTT amplification effects of proxies and chunking.
- Test HTTP/3/QUIC for streaming (expected to reduce head-of-line blocking and lower p99).
- Evaluate bfloat16 compressed token payloads impact on serialization and chunking performance.

Appendix: short run notes and oddities observed:
- On one run we saw a sudden p99 spike correlated with Envoy worker GC (file descriptor churn) — further logs attached to JIRA ticket.
- Python client showed worse syscalls compared to Go client; production SDK should use batching-friendly internals.

Action items (owners):
- Alex Kim: add Envoy config CI benchmark (JIRA: SERV-1234) — due 2025-12-10
- Jordan Li: SDK client windowing POC (JS/Python) + benchmark — due 2025-12-08
- Priya Patel: add per-chunk observability events in runtime (proposal PR) — draft by 2025-12-05

Notes: raw CSVs, perf graphs, and experiment scripts are attached in the linked PR and Confluence page. Use the Confluence page (confluence:SERV-RT-networking-bench-2025) for deep-dive plots and raw numbers.

End of doc.
